title: Integrating single-cell sQTL mapping with deep-learning splicing prediction identifies causal variants under influenza infection.
data_url: Three open sources, all of which I opened. (1) Ten supplementary tables attached to the article, CC-BY-4.0, at https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1186%2Fs13059-026-04205-9/MediaObjects/13059_2026_4205_MOESM1_ESM.xlsx through MOESM10 (49,096,979 bytes total; nine spreadsheets plus one 152,449-byte comma-separated file, plus a 16,063,295-byte figure PDF). (2) GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) series GSE335087, two 10x Genomics single-cell RNA-sequencing gene-count matrices (493,086,720-byte tar; the two .mtx.gz matrices alone are 287,944,458 and 204,381,853 bytes) - file list and metadata checked, matrices NOT downloaded. (3) The preprint version of the same work, free and full-text in Europe PMC as PMC12803322 (CC-BY), which I used for the Methods and the Data availability statement. Genotypes are the public 1000 Genomes 30x NYGC call set (no application needed).

verified.what_i_actually_checked: The paper is real: Europe PMC returned exactly 1 hit for the DOI (PMID 42471654, Genome Biology, first published 2026-07-18, licence CC-BY-4.0 per Crossref). The journal version is NOT in PubMed Central (isOpenAccess 'N', inPMC 'N', the PMC identifier converter says 'Identifier not found in PMC'), and the Springer landing page bounced me to a login redirect, so I read the Methods from the preprint version instead, which IS open full text in Europe PMC (PMID 41542048, PMC12803322, DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-8408992/v1, CC-BY). I downloaded all ten supplementary tables (49,096,979 bytes) and parsed every sheet myself with a stdlib spreadsheet reader, counting rows and columns rather than trusting captions. Verified counts: Table S1 (2,350,575 bytes) has 27,149 data rows and 9 columns (GeneName, GroupID, FeatureID, FeatureLabel, psi(scHH3Uninfected), psi(scHHDCA09), p-value, q-value, dPSI), 27,149 distinct junction labels (zero duplicates), 3,746 genes, 5,576 splice clusters, 24 chromosomes. Table S3 (10,901,381 bytes) has two sheets: 'Uninfected' 53,292 rows / 20 columns / 25,035 distinct variants / 317 genes / 597 junctions, and 'CA09' 43,015 rows / 20,555 distinct variants / 217 genes / 411 junctions. Union across conditions: 28,674 distinct variants, 378 genes - both exactly the numbers in the preprint text. Table S5 (12,569,504 bytes): 'LRT' 41,982 rows / 29 columns, 'CA09_Induced' 1,185 rows, 'Ztest' 41,831 rows; the response-sQTL label column re_sQTL reads 'Constitutive' 34,716 / 'rsQTL' 1,033 / blank 6,082, and 1,033 + 1,185 induced = 2,218 against the paper's 2,217. Table S6 (5,124,807 bytes): 29,342 rows, 28,674 distinct variants, SpliceAI maximum delta score numeric in only 13,315 rows (the other 16,027 read 'NA'), Pangolin numeric in 18,392; a second sheet holds exactly 76 variants in 64 genes. Table S7 (1,553,818 bytes): exactly 57 variants in 51 genes, and a 126-variant looser set - the paper's headline 57. Four checks I computed myself, which are the useful part: (a) dPSI equals psi(CA09) minus psi(uninfected) to within 1e-6 in all 27,149 rows, zero exceptions; (b) of those 27,149 junctions, 12,657 have q-value <= 0.05 but only 783 have an absolute dPSI of 0.05 or more, i.e. significance is driven by cell counts, not effect size; (c) the z_score column matches the standard formula (slope_uninfected - slope_IAV) / sqrt(se_IAV^2 + se_unf^2) in 41,831 of 41,831 rows and matches the equation printed in the Methods in 0 of 41,831 rows, so the printed equation is a typesetting error and the numbers are right; (d) joining Table S3 'CA09' to Table S6 on variant_id matched 20,872 of 29,342 rows, of which 8,422 carry both AI scores, and across those 8,422 the Spearman rank correlation between measured absolute sQTL effect size and SpliceAI maximum delta score is 0.084, and 0.0995 for Pangolin, while SpliceAI and Pangolin agree with each other at 0.611. Mean absolute slope is 1.143 for the 92 variants with SpliceAI >= 0.2 versus 1.016 for the 8,330 below - same direction as the authors' claim, tiny magnitude. (e) Across the 41,831 pairs measured in both conditions, Pearson correlation between infected and uninfected effect sizes is 0.9829 with only 203 sign flips (0.49%). For GEO I read the file list and the series matrix for GSE335087 (two samples, GSM9805660 'scHH2_CA09' and GSM9805661 'scHH1_CA09', both infected, 10x 3-prime v3.1, CellRanger v7.0.1, GRCh38) and for the earlier scHi-HOST series GSE205796 (five samples: three PR8-infected, two mock); I downloaded no sequencing data and no count matrix.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the wet-lab work and the pipeline, taken from the open preprint rather than the journal version: 31,155 uninfected and 13,794 CA09-infected cells; two sequencing batches of 48 cell lines each; droplet-to-donor assignment by Demuxlet; 96 pseudobulk BAM files; junction counting with RegTools v0.5.1 and clustering with LeafCutter v0.2.9; mapping with TensorQTL v1.0.6 within a 100 kb window using two genotype principal components, sex and three PEER factors; SpliceAI scores taken from Illumina's precomputed genome_scores_v1.3 table and Pangolin v1.0.2 run locally with a +/-100 bp window; AlphaGenome v0.4 used with ontology terms EFO:0000572 (lymphoblastoid cell line) and EFO:0008952 (lung). Also text-only: the CRISPR and immunoblot validation of rs2297616 in PARP2, the 13-amino-acid isoform difference, the influenza burden association, and the colocalisation with anti-HSV-1 antibody levels. I could not verify three things at all. First, the per-cell-line junction-ratio matrix and the full nominal association results are deposited nowhere - only the significant SNP-junction pairs are, so there is no set of tested-but-not-significant variants in any file. Second, the uninfected single-cell data behind the 'scHH3Uninfected' column of Table S1 is not in GSE335087, which contains only the two infected samples; the preprint points to the previous publication for it, and I could not match it to a specific sample in GSE205796 (whose uninfected samples are labelled scHH_LGC_Uninfected and were infected with a different strain, PR8). Third, I never saw the journal version's own Data availability statement; the preprint's says only that large files 'will be made available from GEO repository upon publication'. No code repository is named anywhere I looked.

a1_downloadable.note: PASSES. No login, no application, no dead link. I downloaded all ten supplementary tables (49,096,979 bytes, CC-BY-4.0) and read the GEO file list for GSE335087 openly. The genotypes are the public 1000 Genomes 30x New York Genome Center call set, not a controlled-access resource. Only the journal article's own HTML is paywalled to me, and the preprint in Europe PMC (PMC12803322) covers the Methods.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: PASSES, several times over, and I counted each one. Table S1 column 'dPSI' is the change in junction usage between conditions (27,149 rows). Table S3 column 'slope' is the measured per-allele effect on junction usage (43,015 rows infected). Table S5 columns 're_sQTL' and 'lmm_rsQTL' are ready-made categorical labels ('Constitutive' 34,716 / 'rsQTL' 1,033). Nothing has to be constructed by joining. The trap is the opposite one: the paper's own headline label, the 57 'causal' variants, is defined by a SpliceAI/Pangolin score threshold - see A8.

a3_inputs_present.note: PASSES but only just, and only for a sequence model. No table contains any sequence; each row gives GRCh38 coordinates plus reference and alternate alleles (variant_id of the form '1:1498608:T:C') or junction coordinates ('chr22:40951476-40953555'). That is one bulk reference-genome download and then purely offline indexing, not thousands of database lookups, so I pass it. What is genuinely absent is any per-individual data: the per-cell-line junction-ratio matrix is not deposited, and neither are the full nominal association results, so the only features that exist in the files are allele frequency and distance to the transcription start site, and there is no set of tested-but-not-significant variants anywhere.

a4_units_stated.note: PASSES. No units column, but nothing is ambiguous and I checked it arithmetically. PSI (percent spliced in) is a proportion between 0 and 1, and dPSI is exactly the difference of the two PSI columns in all 27,149 rows (zero exceptions at a tolerance of 1e-6). 'slope' is the effect per allele copy on the quantile-normalised intron-excision ratio, and the Methods state the quantile normalisation, so it is a standardised, unitless effect size. 'af' is a frequency, 'tss_distance' is in base pairs, SpliceAI and Pangolin delta scores are probabilities between 0 and 1.

a5_enough_rows.note: PASSES on the one task where the row is the unit, and is an A5-in-disguise failure on the others. Table S1 is genuinely 27,149 junctions, one row each, spread over 3,746 genes - comfortably above the 1,500 floor. But the sQTL tables are 43,015 rows resting on only 217 genes and 411 junctions, and the variants inside a gene are in linkage disequilibrium, so the effect size is a property of a whole haplotype block rather than of the row. The infection-response label is worse: 1,033 positives concentrated in 56 genes. The 57 causal variants are far too few to train anything.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 49,096,979 bytes of supplementary tables that I already parsed in 3.1 seconds, plus roughly 0.9 GB for a one-time GRCh38 reference genome download to pull sequence windows. Nothing else is needed; the 493 MB GEO count-matrix tar and the raw sequencing reads are irrelevant to every framing I considered.
a6_fits_laptop.note: PASSES easily. Peak memory stays near 2 GB if you hold one chromosome at a time, and the baseline is a linear or tree model on cached embeddings, so no GPU.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: PASSES, and unusually tightly - this is the best part of the deposit. From my own counts: 43,015 infected SNP-junction pairs against the abstract's 'approximately 43,000'; 217 genes against '217 genes'; 28,674 distinct variants and 378 genes across both conditions, exactly the preprint's '28,674 sQTLs from 378 sGenes'; 34,716 constitutive sQTLs exactly; 41,831 matched pairs exactly; exactly 76 variants in the both-tools set and exactly 57 in the fine-mapped set. Two tiny discrepancies, both recorded: 1,033 z-test plus 1,185 induced is 2,218 against the stated 2,217, and 6,082 rows of the response table have a blank label that no caption explains. Separately, the z-test equation printed in the Methods matches 0 of 41,831 rows while the standard formula matches all 41,831 - the numbers are right, the printed equation is a typo.

a8_label_provenance.note: PASSES for the labels I would use and FAILS for the paper's headline label, which is the distinction that matters here. dPSI and slope trace back to counted RNA sequencing reads crossing each junction (RegTools counts, LeafCutter ratios, TensorQTL regression on genotypes) - physical measurements, not a model's output. But the 57 and 76 'causal' variant sets are defined by thresholding SpliceAI and Pangolin delta scores at 0.2, so they are literally the output of two deep-learning models; training anything to predict membership in that set would be distilling SpliceAI, with its accuracy as the ceiling. Two further warnings. The response-sQTL labels are thresholded statistical test results rather than measurements, and I showed the two conditions correlate at 0.9829, so those calls sit in the noise tail of a near-identical pair of measurements. And because only significant pairs were deposited, any 'is this a splicing variant' classifier built from these files would have no true negatives.

B1.why: Ten files, seventeen sheets; main task uses one sheet, and the variant_id join matched 20,872 of 29,342 rows (checked).

B2.why: Every sheet has a caption row above the header; Table S6 has two columns differing only in capitalisation (checked).

B3.why: One LeafCutter plus TensorQTL run, author-normalised; dPSI equals the PSI difference in all 27,149 rows (checked).

B4.why: Table S1 has zero missing values, but SpliceAI reads NA in 16,027 of 29,342 rows and 6,082 response labels are blank (checked).

B5.why: Table S1: 27,149 unique junction labels in 27,149 rows; Table S6 has 668 repeated variants (checked).

B6.why: Methods describe the pipeline in detail, but no data dictionary; 'cs', 'as_dist' and the blank labels are undocumented (checked).

C1.why: 'Do splice-prediction models track measured effect sizes in infected immune cells?' is informative either way.

C2.why: SpliceAI, Pangolin, AbSplice, SpliceTransformer and AlphaGenome are all open and already honestly benchmarked (retrieved).

C3.why: Infection-responsive angle is real but thin: 56 response genes, and stimulated-macrophage sQTLs already cover it (retrieved).

C4.why: Generating the data needs a 96-cell-line infection plus CRISPR, but the prediction step is already cheap and solved.

C5.why: SpliceAI and Pangolin scores sit in Table S6, plus published numbers (Pangolin AUPRC 0.85) to compare against.

D1.why: Open-weight DNA sequence models fit this data type: HyenaDNA, DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer all downloadable.

D2.why: Roughly 27,000 junction windows of 1-2 kb; embeddings cache once on CPU, then a linear head.

D3.why: Data is CC-BY-4.0 (Crossref, checked); HyenaDNA and DNABERT-2 weights are permissively licensed.

E1.why: Hold out whole genes (3,746 in Table S1) or chromosomes (24 present) to stop linkage leakage (checked).

E2.why: 3,746 gene groups in Table S1, 217 in the infected sQTL table, 24 chromosomes (all counted in files).

E3.why: Global mean dPSI, per-gene mean dPSI and majority class are all trivially computable from the deposited columns.

E4.why: Infected versus uninfected effect sizes correlate at 0.9829 over 41,831 pairs - a usable ceiling (I computed it).

E5.why: rs2297616 in PARP2 was CRISPR-validated by the authors and must rank near the top; SpliceAI-Pangolin agreement 0.611.

E6.why: Shuffle dPSI within gene, ablate to plain sequence composition, swap embeddings for same-shape random noise.

E7.why: GTEx v8 sQTL (49 tissues), stimulated-macrophage sQTLs (PMC12391537) and the authors' own PR8 series GSE205796 (retrieved).

E8.why: I already reproduced four published counts exactly: 28,674 variants, 378 genes, 34,716 constitutive, 57 causal.

G1.why: rsID in 27,929 of 29,342 rows, GRCh38 chr:pos:ref:alt, Ensembl gene IDs, junction coordinates (all seen in files).

G2.why: GTEx v8 sQTL catalogue joins on variant and gene; GWAS Catalog and Open Targets join on rsID.

G3.why: Variant-to-junction is one-to-many (43,015 pairs for 20,555 variants) and junction definitions differ between datasets.

G4.why: Asks whether infection-only splicing variants are the ones tissue catalogues and sequence models both miss.

H1.why: dPSI has both directions and null junctions; the response label has 34,716 negatives against 1,033 positives (counted).

H2.why: One lab, one cell type (Epstein-Barr-virus-transformed B cells), one virus strain; 96 donors from six populations.

H3.why: The honest claim can be written in one sentence - see honest_claim_h3 - and it is narrow but precise.

H4.why: The preprint states the read-depth limit (2.5% detection at mean depth) and the 96-sample power limit explicitly.

I1.why: Named users: the Gagneur lab (AbSplice), the Li lab (Pangolin, LeafCutter), ClinGen's splicing subgroup.

I2.why: A weak correlation would temper reliance on delta scores for common variants, but similar caveats are already published.

I3.why: The real decision is 'which variant in this credible set is causal' - a top-1 ranking, not the rank correlation I can compute.

I4.why: Sequence-to-splicing is genuinely complex, but the measured 0.084 correlation says little sequence signal is left here.

J1.why: Frozen-backbone plus head with grouped splits is real, but the main deliverable is a benchmark table, not a model.

J2.why: Splicing and linkage-disequilibrium intuition is needed to judge a null; the PARP2 positive control helps.

J3.why: The SpliceAI-versus-measured-effect-size table is already a shareable result; I produced it in 3 seconds.

J4.why: Implicitly one to two weeks; no budget written down anywhere.

existing_models.name: SpliceAI (Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019) - a convolutional neural network that predicts splice-site gain and loss from DNA sequence
existing_models.score_and_split: Code and weights are public (github.com/Illumina/SpliceAI) and Illumina also distributes a precomputed genome-wide score table, which is exactly what these authors used (genome_scores_v1.3, GRCh38). In an independent Genome Biology 2023 benchmark against massively parallel splicing assays, SpliceAI and Pangolin were the two methods with the highest agreement with measured splicing effects (retrieved as a search result; I did not open the paper body, so I verified no exact number). Its delta scores are already sitting in this paper's Table S6, where I found them numeric for 13,315 of 29,342 rows.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved from the original paper. This paper's authors name the gap for me, and it is the most useful sentence in the whole manuscript: 'Using deep learning to systematically discover common genetic causal variants influencing alternative splicing has received less attention', and their hypothesis that the tools favour large-effect variants 'needs further systematic evaluation in future work'.

existing_models.name: Pangolin (Zeng and Li, Genome Biology 2022) - a sequence model predicting tissue-specific splice-site usage
existing_models.score_and_split: Open code (github.com/tkzeng/Pangolin); these authors installed v1.0.2 and ran it themselves. Published numbers from the search results: average top-1 accuracy 79% and area under the precision-recall curve 0.85, against 75% and 0.77 for SpliceAI. Notably, Pangolin's own paper already did the sQTL check this paper repeats - for 57% of sQTLs tested Pangolin picked a causal SNP within one order of magnitude of the lead variant's p-value, versus 53% for SpliceAI and 31% for random SNPs, rising to 87% on its 106 most confident loci. I read these in search snippets, not in the paper body.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved - I read summaries rather than the discussion.

existing_models.name: AbSplice (Wagner et al., Nature Genetics 2023) - combines sequence-model scores with tissue-specific splice-site usage maps
existing_models.score_and_split: Open code at github.com/gagneurlab/absplice. Trained and evaluated on an aberrant-splicing benchmark of over 8.8 million rare variants across 49 GTEx tissues; reported threefold precision improvement at 20% recall over sequence-only baselines, reaching 60% precision when RNA sequencing from accessible tissues is added. Numbers from the search summary, not from the paper body. This is the closest competitor to anything one could build here, because it already solves the tissue-specific version of the problem using GTEx sQTLs.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved. A follow-up preprint on aberrant splicing during organ development appeared in 2025, which suggests the authors themselves see developmental and context-specific coverage as the open edge.

existing_models.name: SpliceTransformer / SpTransformer (You et al., Nature Communications 2024) - a transformer predicting tissue-specific splicing in 15 human tissues
existing_models.score_and_split: Open code at github.com/ShenLab-Genomics/SpliceTransformer. Reported to outperform previous methods on splicing prediction and applied to about 1.3 million ClinVar variants, concluding that splicing changes explain 60% of intronic and synonymous pathogenic mutations. Retrieved as search summaries with a PubMed and a PMC record (PMC11500173); I did not open the paper, so no split is verified.

existing_models.name: AlphaGenome (Google DeepMind, 2025) - a sequence-to-function model that includes splice-site usage and splice-junction outputs
existing_models.score_and_split: No score verified by me. Relevant because this paper's own Methods say they ran AlphaGenome v0.4 with ontology terms EFO:0000572 (lymphoblastoid cell line) and EFO:0008952 (lung), feeding it 1 Mb of sequence per variant - so the newest and largest model has already been pointed at this exact dataset by its own authors, which removes most of the headroom a new model would have.

existing_models.name: Context for the diversity angle: stimulated-macrophage sQTL mapping (Nature Communications 2025, PMC12391537, PMID 40866368)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not a model, but it is the reason the 'nobody has looked at condition-specific splicing' angle is weaker than it first appears. Retrieved via search: sQTL mapping in macrophages across a wide range of stimuli, with effects reported for over 5,734 genes, linking low-usage splice junctions to immune-mediated disease risk. That is roughly twenty-five times the gene count of this paper's 217, in a primary immune cell type, and it is open access. It is the best external validation set available and simultaneously the main competitor for the angle.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved beyond the summary, which frames low-usage junctions as the under-studied part.

backbone.name: HyenaDNA (open weights, Apache-2.0, handles long context) or DNABERT-2 as the frozen encoder of the 1-2 kb window around each splice junction, with a ridge or gradient-boosted head predicting dPSI. SpliceAI and Pangolin are the comparison baselines rather than backbones - their scores are already in Table S6, so the comparison costs nothing.
backbone.hardware: About 27,000 windows of 1-2 kb for the junction task (or 41,000 reference-and-alternate pairs for the variant task). On a 16 GB CPU laptop that is roughly 2-4 hours of one-time embedding, cached to disk once; the head then trains in seconds. No GPU.
backbone.licence: Clean. The article and its supplementary tables are CC-BY-4.0 (confirmed in Crossref metadata). HyenaDNA and DNABERT-2 weights are permissive; Nucleotide Transformer is CC-BY-NC (non-commercial) if used instead. One caveat worth flagging: Illumina's precomputed SpliceAI score table is distributed under an academic-use licence, but the delta scores needed here are already inside the CC-BY supplement.

integration.partner_dataset: GTEx v8 (or v10) splicing-QTL summary statistics across 49 human tissues - the same LeafCutter-based pipeline this paper adapted, so the phenotype definitions are comparable. Secondary partners: the GWAS Catalog and Open Targets on rsID, and the stimulated-macrophage sQTL resource (PMC12391537).
integration.join_key: variant_id in GRCh38 chr:pos:ref:alt form, present in every row, plus rsID (present in 27,929 of 29,342 rows of Table S6; 1,413 read 'NA'), plus Ensembl gene identifiers. I verified the internal variant_id join works: 20,872 of 29,342 Table S6 rows matched a variant in the infected sQTL table.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Are the splicing variants that act only during infection the same ones that tissue-level catalogues such as GTEx systematically miss, and do sequence-based splice predictors miss them for the same reason? Neither dataset answers that alone - but the infection-specific set here is only 56 genes, and I measured the infected and uninfected effect sizes to correlate at 0.9829, so there is very little condition-specific signal to join on.

controls.positive_control: Three, and two are cheap. rs2297616 in PARP2 must rank near the top of any causal-variant score: the authors CRISPR-edited it and showed it creates a 5-prime splice donor adding 13 amino acids, and it ranked 5th by splice score in their own analysis. Second, a trivially learnable target: predict intron length from the sequence window, which must come out near-perfect or the plumbing is wrong. Third, as a plumbing check on the two score columns, SpliceAI and Pangolin must agree with each other - I measured Spearman 0.611 across 8,422 variants, so that check already passes.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle dPSI within gene and confirm performance collapses to the per-gene mean - essential here, because junctions in one gene share sequence context. Ablate the embedding and keep only plain sequence composition (GC content, splice-site motif match); if composition does as well, the language model adds nothing. Replace embeddings with same-shape random noise and confirm it matches the dummy. Finally, re-split at random instead of by gene and watch the score inflate, which measures how much linkage leakage a careless split buys you.
controls.external_validation: Three real options. GTEx v8 sQTL across 49 tissues, which the authors already used for a replication statistic, so I would be extending their own check. The stimulated-macrophage sQTL resource (Nature Communications 2025, PMC12391537, over 5,734 genes) - a different immune cell type, different stimuli, open access. And the authors' own earlier experiment in GEO series GSE205796, which used influenza strain PR8 rather than CA09, giving a held-out virus strain. There is no publication-year column, so the cheap temporal split is unavailable.

honest_claim_h3: Among splice junctions already detectable in 3-prime-biased single-cell RNA sequencing of 96 Epstein-Barr-virus-transformed B-cell lines, local DNA sequence explains X percent of the variance in how much junction usage shifts after influenza A infection - a shift whose median size is below one percentage point, measured once per junction with no replicate, in one cell type, one virus strain and one laboratory.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the DNA sequence around a splice junction to predict how much that junction's use shifts when cells are infected with influenza.
plain_idea.train_on: One row per splice junction: roughly 1-2 kilobases of human reference DNA (build GRCh38) around the junction, turned into numbers by a frozen DNA language model. I counted 27,149 junctions in 3,746 genes in the deposited table, with no duplicates.
plain_idea.predict: The change in that junction's usage between uninfected and influenza-infected cells, measured as a difference in PSI (percent spliced in, the fraction of transcripts that use the junction). The true answer comes from counting RNA sequencing reads that cross each junction in pooled single-cell data from 96 human B-cell lines - a real measurement, not another model's output.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: The people who build splice-prediction tools (the AbSplice and Pangolin groups) and the clinical geneticists who use them would learn whether infection-responsive splicing is written into local DNA sequence at all. Even a clear null is useful: it would say that which junctions respond to infection is set by cell state rather than by sequence.

ml_idea: Four framings, and the verified numbers argue against all four as a project while making one of them a good one-day note. (1) Sequence to infection-induced splicing change. Table S1 is the cleanest thing in the deposit - 27,149 junctions, one row each, zero duplicates, zero missing values, dPSI exactly equal to the difference of the two PSI columns in every row - so a frozen DNA-language-model head with gene-held-out splits is easy to build. The problem is the label: 12,657 junctions have a q-value below 0.05 but only 783 have an absolute dPSI of 0.05 or more, so the significance is manufactured by treating 45,000 cells as independent replicates while the real effects are below one percentage point, measured once, with no replicate deposited to estimate the noise floor. (2) Sequence to measured sQTL effect size. This is the framing the paper invites, and it is the one I tested: joining the infected sQTL table to the AI-score table on variant identifier gave 8,422 variants with both scores, and the Spearman correlation between measured absolute effect size and SpliceAI's maximum delta score is 0.084 (Pangolin 0.0995), with mean absolute slope 1.143 for the 92 variants above the 0.2 threshold versus 1.016 for the 8,330 below. The direction matches the authors' claim; the magnitude says there is almost nothing for a new sequence model to capture, and in any case the label belongs to a whole linkage-disequilibrium block rather than to the row. (3) Classify infection-responsive versus constitutive sQTLs. The labels are ready-made ('Constitutive' 34,716, 'rsQTL' 1,033, plus 1,185 induced in a separate sheet), but the positives sit in only 56 genes, 6,082 rows carry a blank label that no caption explains, and I measured the infected and uninfected effect sizes to correlate at 0.9829 with 0.49% sign flips - so the response calls are the noise tail of two nearly identical measurements. (4) Predict the 57 'causal' variants. This fails outright on provenance: that set is defined by thresholding SpliceAI and Pangolin at 0.2, so a model trained on it would be distilling SpliceAI. What is genuinely worth a day, and what I would send to the authors, is the systematic evaluation they themselves call for in their discussion: a table of measured sQTL effect size against SpliceAI, Pangolin and AlphaGenome scores, stratified by fine-mapping posterior and by whether the variant is the lead SNP, with the honest caveat that only significant pairs were deposited so there are no true negatives. Two file-level findings belong in the same note: the z-test equation printed in the Methods matches 0 of 41,831 rows while the standard formula matches all 41,831 (the numbers are right, the equation is a typo), and SpliceAI scores are missing for 16,027 of 29,342 annotated variants, which is 55% of the table the headline rests on.

effort.compute_note: The table side is timed, not estimated: downloading all ten supplementary files took under a minute, and my parsing script read five workbooks, counted 180,000-odd rows across seventeen sheets, and computed every correlation in this evaluation in 3.1 seconds of CPU time, under 1 GB of memory. The remaining five hours are an estimate for downloading GRCh38, extracting 27,149 sequence windows and joining them to the labels. The three embedding hours are an estimate, not a timing: about 27,000 windows of 1-2 kb at a few windows per second for a small DNA language model on this CPU.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: The one I already ran, and it took three seconds: join the infected sQTL sheet of Table S3 to Table S6 on variant_id, keep the 8,422 variants that carry both AI scores, and compute the Spearman correlation between measured absolute effect size and SpliceAI's maximum delta score. It is 0.084 (Pangolin 0.0995), with mean absolute slope 1.143 above the 0.2 threshold against 1.016 below. Second-cheapest, one more minute: correlate slope_IAV against slope_Unf in Table S5 - 0.9829 over 41,831 pairs - which shows there is almost no condition-specific signal for an infection-response model to learn.

verdict_reason: All eight Part A killers pass, and I verified them in the files rather than from the abstract - this is the rare case where the deposit matches the paper almost exactly (43,015 infected SNP-junction pairs, 217 genes, 28,674 variants and 378 genes across conditions, 34,716 constitutive sQTLs, exactly 57 and exactly 76 causal variants, all counted by me). It still fails as a project, for three reasons that the files settle. First, C2 is a zero: SpliceAI, Pangolin, AbSplice, SpliceTransformer and AlphaGenome are all open, reproducible and already honestly benchmarked against massively parallel splicing assays, and the authors ran three of them on this very dataset, so there is no headroom left. Second, model-readiness is 7 of 12, below the threshold, because what was deposited is summary statistics: the per-cell-line junction-ratio matrix is absent, the full nominal association results are absent (so there are no tested-but-not-significant variants anywhere, hence no true negatives), SpliceAI reads NA in 16,027 of 29,342 rows, and 6,082 response labels are blank with no explanation. Third, and decisively, I measured the signal the project would depend on and it is not there: across 8,422 variants carrying both AI scores, the Spearman correlation between measured absolute sQTL effect size and SpliceAI's maximum delta score is 0.084 (Pangolin 0.0995), and across the 41,831 pairs measured in both conditions the infected and uninfected effect sizes correlate at 0.9829 with only 203 sign flips, so the 'infection-responsive' category is the noise tail of two near-identical measurements and sits in only 56 genes. The cleanest table, Table S1, is clean but weakly informative: 27,149 junctions with dPSI exactly equal to the PSI difference in every row, yet 12,657 are called significant while only 783 move by five percentage points or more, which is pseudo-replication across cells rather than biology, and no replicate is deposited to estimate the noise floor. Note that the computed return-on-investment will look flattering here because the effort is genuinely tiny (49 MB of spreadsheets, 3.1 seconds to parse, no GPU) and integration and backbone fit score well (7 of 8 and 6 of 6) - that is a real property of the data, not a reason to do it. Three things are worth keeping. The deposit is unusually honest and I reproduced four of its headline counts exactly, which makes it a good external test set for anyone else's splicing model. A one-day note is genuinely publishable-adjacent and answers a question the authors themselves pose in their discussion ('this hypothesis needs further systematic evaluation in future work'): the three numbers above, plus the observation that the z-test equation printed in the Methods matches 0 of 41,831 rows while the standard formula matches all of them. And the positive control is excellent - rs2297616 in PARP2 was CRISPR-validated - so if a future deposit includes the per-individual junction matrices, this moves from reject to verify_first immediately. If I were to spend time on it anyway, the kill condition would be: if by day three the gene-held-out correlation between predicted and measured dPSI is below 0.15, stop.
